1:
Wisdom builds before she invites. Delitzsch reads the perfects as an inventory of everything she has already done to prepare, and notes that the picture is not quite a parable: had it been, the verbs would have run into the historical narrative form, but the imperfect of "she crieth" shows an allegory of a present reality rather than a story. He observes that the Hebrew for wisdom here is plural, a plural of excellence, an expression of plural unity that takes a singular predicate as the common word for God does; and that the text does not say she built a house for herself but that she built her house, the dwelling being hers already in its origin.

What the house is divides the commentators sharply. Gill catalogues the guesses, from the circle of the sciences with the seven liberal arts for pillars, to the schools of the prophets, to the universe with the seven days of creation or the seven planets, to the odd proposal of the human body with its five senses plus voice and memory, before settling on the human nature of Christ, a temple built without the hands of men, its seven pillars the graces of the Spirit. Henry hears the Word of God speaking, and takes the house to be at once heaven, the Father's house of many mansions, and the church supported by the power and promise of God as by seven pillars; he thinks Solomon may have had in view the temple he had lately built. Ellicott first sets the whole scene in a known idiom, noting that Scripture regularly describes communion with God and the refreshment the soul receives from it under the figure of a festival, as when the elders of Israel saw God and did eat and drink. He then makes the two senses explicit: Christ built his house by taking man's flesh at the Incarnation, and builds it still as the spiritual house that is the church. Wesley keeps it plain, seven meaning many, and the pillars prophets, apostles and ministers.

Clarke refuses the whole procedure. Having listed the standard allegory, with the seven pillars as the seven sacraments or the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit, the slain beasts as the sacrifice of the cross, and the bread and mingled wine as the elements of the Supper, he dismisses it as strange creatures of the interpreters' own brain, and holds instead that the eternal counsel of God has framed the universe, everything constructed to exhibit grandeur, stability and durableness. Where Gill reads the killed beasts as a crucified Christ offered vicariously and never to be repeated, Clarke reads them as God's ample provision for the innumerable tribes of creatures that people created nature.

The slaughter is contested at the level of the word. Henry presses that the term is sacrifice, making this a sumptuous but sacred feast, a feast upon a sacrifice. Delitzsch says the opposite: this noun, as distinguished from the ordinary sacrificial term, is the usual word for slaughter outside the sacrificial system, and the slain beast is simply an ox. He declines to allegorize the menu at all, since flesh and wine are figures of the nourishment found with wisdom and one should not ask what each specially means, and takes the seven pillars for the virtues of her own nature communicating themselves. Ellicott adds that the mingled wine was probably flavoured with spices to improve it, while noting that Passover wine was mingled with water to decrease its strength. Henry, for his part, will not stop at the furniture: the table is furnished with everything a soul can desire, righteousness and grace, peace and joy, the assurances of God's love and the earnests of eternal life, and he presses that it is all Wisdom's own doing, since she killed the beasts and mingled the wine herself rather than leaving the preparation to others.
3:
The maidens are the first point of dispute. Gill denies they are moral virtues, the liberal arts, or angels, and identifies them as ministers of the Gospel, adding carefully that the figure does not encourage women's preaching but keeps the decency of the parable, a lady of rank being properly attended by maidens. Their voice, he says, is not the rough voice of the law but the still, small, musical voice of the Gospel. Wesley says the same in a line and glosses the high places as the seats from which judges delivered sentence. Ellicott notes that the same errand in the parable of the king's son is given to servants rather than maidens, and that the crying from the highest places answers to the command to proclaim upon the housetops. Clarke supplies a custom rather than a doctrine: in Asiatic countries invitations are still carried to the guests' doors by a company of women.

Delitzsch marks where the allegory gives way. The maidens retire into the background, Wisdom appears in her own person, and the discourse is interrupted by a narrator's aside, "she saith to him" — signs, he judges, that the pure execution of the allegorical representation has come to an end. He records that Hitzig tried to secure a logical sequence by cutting out this verse and the next, and answers that the interpolations so removed are far harder to account for than the text as it stands. On the invitation itself he observes that "who is simple" is only a more animated way of saying "whoever is simple," and that the plural address shows the simple and the heartless to be one class rather than two.

The bread and wine draw out the difference in temper. Gill takes the bread for the whole provision of Christ's house, everything else being what the prophet called that which is not bread: the Gospel, the Supper, and chiefly Christ himself, eaten by faith and eaten daily as Israel ate manna. Clarke turns the same words into a charge to study: act on the directions, go by the streams to the fountain head, examine the properties and relations of things and see the goodness of God in them, and then learn how little you know. He quotes Pope on drinking deep or not tasting at all, surveys the ancient proportions of water to wine, and concludes that the mingled wine was probably not diluted but strengthened with spices. Wesley had said flatly that it was mingled with water, as they used to do in those hot countries.

The closing summons is read two ways. Gill, Clarke and Wesley take it as a command to abandon bad company, since the companion of fools must be a fool, and Gill extends it to foolish things as well, noting that the versions render the word as foolishness, imprudence, or want of judgment. Delitzsch prefers to read the plural as a vocative, on the ground that it is a singular thought that the simple should leave the simple, so that Wisdom is telling the simple themselves to leave off; others, he records, take the word as an abstract noun. Ellicott agrees that it means the simple, and hears a call to stop being counted among the weak who are carried about with every wind of doctrine. On the invitation itself he had already observed that God does not call many wise after the flesh, but chooses the foolish and the weak and the base whom men overlook, being unwilling that any should perish, and least of all the little ones who are liable to fall through inexperience. Gill reads the turning in hither two ways at once, as entering a school where Father, Son and Spirit teach, and as turning aside into an inn, since the saints are travellers far from their Father's house and here find room, rest and provision free of cost.
7:
The rule about scorners is felt as a hard one. Gill takes it as the limit of the invitation: the simple may be called in, but not the haughty scorner who mocks at all religion and is irreclaimable, and he applies it historically, since the Jews were first invited to the feast, made light of it, and the maidens were then bid to turn to the Gentiles. He extends the scorner in the next verse to the Pharisees whom Christ told his disciples to let alone, and remarks that ministers of the word are for this reason of all men most hated. Wesley makes the connection backwards explicit: the scorners and wicked men here are precisely the foolish whose company the previous verse told the simple to forsake, since no good but only hurt was to be got from them. Ellicott reads the same restraint into our Lord's method of teaching in parables so that his hearers should not understand, and glosses the shame as insult.

Clarke will not let the saying become a licence. The scorner, he says, is the libertine and the infidel who turns serious things into ridicule and by his wit often makes the reprover ridiculous; it is vain to try to mend such a man by reproof, and yet we must not suffer sin upon our neighbour, but at all hazards deliver our own soul. No reproof should ever be given except in the spirit of love and deep concern, and only when they contradict and blaspheme are they to be left to God. Delitzsch guards the saying at another point. One commentator had made it the ground of the summons to forsake bad company, which requires treating the scorner and the simple as one category, and Delitzsch objects that this confounds two sharply distinguished classes, the freethinker who mocks at religion and virtue being a different man from the godless. He adds a small grammatical observation with a large edge: the connecting letter in "and he will love thee" states a consequence, not a purpose, so the point is not that you reprove in order to be loved.

Delitzsch is at his best on the wise man's teachableness. He calls attention to the interchange of wise and just within a single verse: wisdom is not merely an intellectual power but a moral quality, and it is on that quality that her receptivity to instruction rests, for she is humble, and without self-will makes God's will her binding rule. Gill notes that the Hebrew says only "give to a wise man," leaving the gift unspecified, whether reproof, correction or doctrine, and that the versions read it instead as giving him occasion to show his wisdom. Clarke puts it in a figure: such men are like the bee, and extract honey from every flower.

The fear of the Lord raises a textual question. Delitzsch treats the plural "holy" as an internally multiplicative plural naming the absolutely Holy One, and Ellicott agrees. Clarke reports the older reading preserved in the versions, where the word is the holy ones, the saints, and the phrase becomes their counsel. On the promise of long life, Gill hears Wisdom giving length of days for ever and ever from her right hand; Clarke makes it a plain consequence, vice shortening life and righteousness lengthening it, and records a long addition here in the Greek, Syriac and Latin about the man who trusts in falsity and feeds on the winds. Delitzsch, holding that the verb must be transitive, finds the agent deliberately concealed, so that they, the heavenly Powers, grant the years in rich measure. On the last verse all agree that wisdom is its own profit and mockery its own disgrace, and Gill notes only that the Greek turns the gain outward, making the man who is wise for himself wise for his neighbours too.
13:
Folly is built as Wisdom's deliberate mirror. Delitzsch says the poet personifies her and gives her a feminine name because the contrast required it, and because seduction appears especially in the form of degraded womanhood; the construction is appositional, the woman who is Folly, and her boisterousness is not incidental but her method, overcoming the mind's resistance by noise. Ellicott adds that she is not of dignified mien like her rival, and that the Hebrew calls her simplicity itself, so that knowing nothing she leaves room for all evil to enter and dwell with her. Clarke, more briskly, observes that vain and empty women make the most noise, and that whoever is full of clamour has generally little sense.

Who she stands for divides them. Henry takes her for carnal sensual pleasure, which defiles the mind, stupefies conscience and puts out the sparks of conviction, and which carries the day by dint of impudence precisely because it has nothing rational to offer. Gill, having listed the same candidates, folly itself, blind reason, sensual pleasure, heresy, the old serpent, settles instead on antichrist, the great whore, and reads the passage as a portrait of Rome, with its boasted infallibility and works of supererogation, its chapels that imitate Wisdom's own words, and its priests as wolves in sheep's clothing. Clarke stays with the general case but sharpens it: Wisdom sets up her school to instruct the ignorant, and Folly sets hers up next door to defeat it, and he quotes the couplet that wherever God erects a house of prayer the devil builds a chapel there, the latter having the larger congregation. Ellicott makes the imitation the point, since Satan too transforms himself into an angel of light, and observes that Folly catches the undecided who are on the right road but lack the constancy to keep it.

Her posture is read as evidence. Gill contrasts her idleness with Wisdom's labour, the building, the killing, the furnishing, the sending out of maidens, where Folly merely exposes herself in public and sits at ease like a queen. Ellicott says she does not care to send anyone out to seek and save what was lost, but contents herself with sitting just outside her own door. Henry catches the same detail and turns it: she sits watching for a prey, not as Abraham at his tent door watching for an opportunity to do good, and the word for her seat means a throne, as though she had authority to give law. Her victims, he says, are the well-educated young who are going right on their ways, and her method is to call them simple for keeping the restraints of their religion. It is the method of the stage, where the sober young man is the fool in the play; but the day will declare who the fools are.

The bait and the reckoning close the chapter. Henry notes that she offers only water and bread where Wisdom offered beasts and mingled wine, and that the whole attraction is that they are stolen, a defiance of the law, since the water is sweeter for being come at through the hedge of the commandment, and of the curse, since the bread is eaten in secret for fear of discovery. Wesley makes it the difficulty of obtaining them, and the prohibition itself rendering them more grateful to corrupt nature. Gill takes the sealed wells of a hot country as the literal ground of the proverb and reads idolatry as the spiritual theft. On the last verse Delitzsch takes the shades to be the worn-out who are alive only in appearance, and insists the phrase means the depths of Hades and not its valleys. Gill and Clarke report the older versions that make them instead the giants of the old world.
